9987.title: Integral Domain
9987.heading: Integral Domain
9987.content:
An integral domain is a nonzero [[Commutative Ring]] in which a product can equal zero only when at least one factor is zero. Equivalently, it has no [[Zero Divisor]]s.

Every [[Field]] is an integral domain, but an integral domain need not make every nonzero element invertible. A proper ideal is a [[Prime Ideal]] exactly when the corresponding [[Quotient Ring]] is an integral domain.

The modern-algebra development uses the absence of zero divisors to prove cancellation and to constrain characteristic. It also proves that every finite integral domain is a field by turning multiplication by a nonzero element into a bijection.

9990.title: Integer
9990.heading: Integer
9990.content:
An integer is a whole number, including zero, a positive natural number, or the [[Opposite Number]] of a positive natural number:

$$\mathbb{Z}=\{\ldots,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,\ldots\}.$$

Integers extend the natural numbers so subtraction always has an integer result. Their signs can be interpreted as opposite directions on a [[Number Line]] or as gains and losses. Addition moves in the direction indicated by each sign, while multiplication by a negative reverses direction. Two sign reversals make a positive product; one makes a negative product.

9992.sourceSearchName: instance based learning framework instance based learning framework
9992.title: Instance-Based Learning Framework
9992.heading: Document

9993.sourceSearchName: instance based learning framework instance based learning framework
9993.title: Instance-Based Learning Framework
9993.heading: Instance-Based Learning Framework
9993.content:
An instance-based learning framework stores training observations and defers most generalization until a test case arrives. It identifies a relevant local neighborhood and predicts from the labels or locally fitted models within it.

This lazy strategy avoids committing to a global boundary, allowing different parts of the feature space to behave differently. Its accuracy and cost depend on the representation, distance function, neighborhood size, and efficiency of retrieving nearby cases.

9994.title: Instance-Based Learning Framework
9994.heading: References

9996.title: Integer Overflow
9996.heading: Integer Overflow
9996.content:
Integer overflow occurs when an arithmetic result lies outside the range of integer values a computer representation can store. A mathematically valid expression can therefore produce an incorrect machine result.

A common [[Binary Search]] implementation calculated the midpoint of lower and upper positions as $(low+high)/2$. Even when both positions were valid, their sum could overflow. The equivalent form $low+(high-low)/2$ avoids forming that excessive intermediate value.

9998.sourceSearchName: instantaneous collision detection instantaneous collision detection
9998.title: Instantaneous Collision Detection
9998.heading: Document

9999.sourceSearchName: instantaneous collision detection instantaneous collision detection
9999.title: Instantaneous Collision Detection
9999.heading: Instantaneous Collision Detection
9999.content:
Instantaneous collision detection tests whether shapes overlap at one sampled moment, usually the current simulation update. It is efficient and sufficient when objects move only a small distance between tests.

A fast object can pass completely through a thin obstacle between frames without overlapping at either sample. [[Continuous Collision Detection]] addresses this tunneling problem by considering the path traveled during the interval.

10002.sourceSearchName: installable web application installable web application
10002.title: Installable Web Application
10002.heading: Installable Web Application
10002.content:
An installable web application can be added to a device's application launcher or home screen without passing through a traditional application store. It remains a web application reached from a URL but can open with app-oriented display behavior.

Installation depends on progressive-web requirements such as a [[Web App Manifest]], suitable icons, a [[Service Worker]], and a [[Secure Origin]].

10003.title: Installable Web Application

10005.title: Insertion Sort
10005.heading: Insertion Sort
10005.content:
Insertion sort processes items one at a time and inserts each new item into its proper position among those already ordered. It resembles maintaining a sorted hand of playing cards as cards arrive.

Its $O(n^2)$ [[Time Complexity]] is not optimal for large arbitrary collections, but it is an [[Online Algorithm]]: it can maintain a valid sorted result without knowing how many later items will arrive.

10007.sourceSearchName: inscribed angle theorem inscribed angle theorem
10007.title: Inscribed Angle Theorem
10007.heading: Document

10008.sourceSearchName: inscribed angle theorem inscribed angle theorem
10008.title: Inscribed Angle Theorem
10008.heading: Inscribed Angle Theorem
10008.content: An inscribed angle has its vertex on a circle and its sides along chords. Its measure is half the measure of the central angle subtending the same arc. Consequently, inscribed angles standing on the same chord are equal, and an angle subtended by a diameter is a right angle.

10009.sourceSearchName: inscribed angle theorem inscribed angle theorem
10009.title: Inscribed Angle Theorem
10009.heading: References

10011.title: Input Density
10011.heading: Input Density
10011.content:
Input density is the amount of meaningful interaction expressed through a compact [[Physical Input Layer]]. A single button can represent several related phases when pressing, holding, and releasing it each have a clear role.

Dense input can reduce hand movement, mispresses, and memorization while keeping important [[Game Verb|verbs]] prominent. Density is useful when the mappings remain coherent; compressing unrelated actions onto one control can instead make the system harder to predict.

10014.title: Input Polling
10014.heading: Input Polling
10014.content:
Input polling queries the current state of a device during the game frame. Keyboard keys, mouse buttons, controller buttons, axes, and triggers are copied into an input-state object that gameplay can inspect.

Polling gives a consistent per-frame snapshot, but edge detection requires comparison with the previous snapshot. Device events may update the same stored state while the rest of the game consumes a stable abstraction.

10017.title: Input Sequence
10017.heading: Input Sequence
10017.content:
An input sequence is an ordered pattern of control activations recognized within timing constraints. Fighting-game combinations and gesture-like button patterns depend on the progression of states rather than simultaneous activation.

The recognizer must track partial progress and reject the pattern when an expected event fails to occur in time. Unlike an [[Input Chord]], sequence meaning is distributed across multiple moments.

10020.title: Input Size
10020.heading: Input Size
10020.content:
Input size is the quantity used to express the scale of a problem instance, conventionally written as $n$. Its meaning depends on the problem: it may be the number of records to sort, vertices in a graph, or digits in a number.

[[Computational Complexity]] relates resource use to this measure rather than treating every input as equivalent. Selecting the relevant dimension is part of modeling the problem because an irrelevant physical property of the data may have no effect on the operations an [[Algorithm]] performs.

10023.title: Input Device
10023.heading: Input Device
10023.content:
An input device is a physical device that allows communication from a user to a computer. It is the hardware used to capture an action; the [[Interaction Technique]] supplies the software mapping that turns the captured data into an effect in the system.

Input can be discrete, such as a button value, continuous, such as a stream of positions, or a combination of both. Important characteristics include [[Degrees of Freedom]], data frequency, whether measurements are absolute or relative, and whether the sensor must be held or worn. A device should be selected together with the task and interaction technique because one device may map naturally to one task and poorly to another.

10026.title: Input Chord
10026.heading: Input Chord
10026.content:
An input chord is a combination of controls that must be active at approximately the same time to represent one command. It treats simultaneous state as meaningful, such as a modifier held while another button is pressed.

Chord recognition differs from an [[Input Sequence]], where order and timing across successive presses matter. Both translate low-level device events into higher-level player actions.

10028.sourceSearchName: input action mapping input action mapping
10028.title: Input Action Mapping
10028.heading: Document

10029.sourceSearchName: input action mapping input action mapping
10029.title: Input Action Mapping
10029.heading: Input Action Mapping
10029.content:
Input action mapping associates logical commands such as jump, fire, or pause with device-specific controls. Gameplay queries the action instead of knowing whether it came from a key, mouse button, controller button, or axis.

The mapping supports remapping and multiple device layouts while preserving one gameplay interface. Digital edges and analog values still need appropriate semantics after several physical inputs are combined into the same action.

10030.sourceSearchName: input action mapping input action mapping
10030.title: Input Action Mapping
10030.heading: References

10032.title: Inner Product
10032.heading: Inner Product
10032.content:
An inner product assigns a scalar $\langle u,v\rangle$ to two vectors while satisfying conjugate symmetry, linearity, and positivity. It generalizes the geometric dot product.

It defines length by $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ and orthogonality by a zero inner product. Different inner products can impose different geometries on the same vector space.

10034.sourceSearchName: inline r code inline r code
10034.title: Inline R Code
10034.heading: Document

10035.sourceSearchName: inline r code inline r code
10035.title: Inline R Code
10035.heading: Inline R Code
10035.content:
Inline R code embeds a small computed value directly within prose. It keeps reported counts, estimates, or dates synchronized with the analysis when the document is rebuilt.

Inline expressions should remain short and rely on objects created in clearly labeled chunks.

10036.sourceSearchName: inline r code inline r code
10036.title: Inline R Code

10037.heading: Document

10038.sourceSearchName: inline css styles inline css styles
10038.title: Inline CSS Styles
10038.heading: Inline CSS Styles
10038.content:
An inline style stores declarations in an element's `style` attribute. Because the declarations are attached directly to one element, no selector is needed and the styling is difficult to reuse across other elements.

Inline declarations receive a dedicated, very strong position in [[CSS Specificity]], although an important declaration can still alter cascade precedence. Inline styles therefore trade structural reuse for a narrowly targeted declaration source.

10041.title: Injective Resolution
10041.heading: Injective Resolution
10041.content:
An injective resolution of a module M is an exact sequence 0 → M → I⁰ → I¹ → ··· in which every Iⁱ is an [[Injective Module]].

Applying Hom into this cocomplex and taking cohomology constructs Ext groups. The minimum possible finite length of such a resolution is the [[Injective Dimension]].

10043.title: Injective Module
10043.heading: Document
10043.content:
2026-09-13 20:00

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Projective Flat and Injective Modules]]

10044.title: Injective Module
10044.heading: Injective Module
10044.content:
An injective module Q has the extension property: whenever N embeds in M, every homomorphism N → Q extends to a homomorphism M → Q.

Injectivity is dual to projectivity. Short exact sequences beginning with an injective module split, and [[Injective Resolution]]s provide one route to defining the [[Ext Functor]].

10046.title: Initialization Vector

10047.title: Initialization Vector
10047.heading: Initialization Vector
10047.content:
An initialization vector supplies varying input to a block-cipher mode so identical plaintext encrypted with the same key does not begin with identical ciphertext. It influences the first block and, through the mode, the blocks that follow.

An IV normally does not need to be secret, but its uniqueness or unpredictability requirements must be respected for the chosen mode. It is commonly stored alongside the ciphertext while the encryption key is protected separately.

10049.title: Injective Function
10049.heading: Document
10049.content:

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Functions and Elementary Number Theory]] · [[Functions Cardinality and Relational Data]]

10050.title: Injective Function
10050.heading: Injective Function
10050.content:
An injective function sends distinct domain elements to distinct outputs. Equivalently, equal outputs imply equal inputs.

An injective homomorphism identifies its source with an isomorphic substructure of the target.

An injection prevents collisions: if f(x) = f(y), then x = y. Comparing infinite sets through injective maps helps establish their relative cardinalities.

10053.title: Initial Ideal
10053.heading: Initial Ideal
10053.content:
The initial ideal of a polynomial ideal I is generated by the leading monomials of all polynomials in I under a fixed [[Monomial Order]]. It converts a general polynomial ideal into a monomial ideal.

A finite subset is a [[Gröbner Basis]] precisely when its leading terms generate the initial ideal. This reduces membership and remainder questions to finitely many leading divisibility tests.

10055.title: Injective Dimension
10055.heading: Document

Tags: [[Projective Flat and Injective Modules]]

10056.title: Injective Dimension
10056.heading: Injective Dimension
10056.content:
The injective dimension of a module is the least length of a finite [[Injective Resolution]], or infinity if none exists. An injective module has injective dimension zero.

For a finitely generated module of finite injective dimension over a Noetherian local ring, the source relates that dimension to the depth of the ring through Ext vanishing.

10059.sourceSearchName: infrastructure as a service infrastructure as a service
10059.title: Infrastructure as a Service
10059.heading: Infrastructure as a Service
10059.content:
Infrastructure as a service provides hardware-oriented computing resources such as servers, storage, and networking on a utility basis. The provider supplies and operates the physical resource pool, while the consumer retains substantial control over the systems and applications placed on it.

Typical uses include computing-intensive work, elastic web hosting, storage, and remote backup. An operating system preinstalled for provider security does not by itself turn IaaS into [[Platform as a Service]]; the distinction depends on whether a usable application platform and supporting software are provided.

10062.title: Initial Cluster Partition
10062.heading: Initial Cluster Partition
10062.content:
An initial cluster partition is the starting allocation of observations or seed representatives used by an iterative method. It can be chosen randomly, constructed from ordered data, or refined through a preliminary algorithm.

Different initial partitions can lead to different local optima. Initialization is therefore part of the model specification and should be varied or justified rather than treated as an invisible implementation detail.

10064.heading: Document

10065.sourceSearchName: infrared optical tracking infrared optical tracking
10065.title: Infrared Optical Tracking
10065.heading: Infrared Optical Tracking
10065.content:
Infrared optical tracking uses cameras and controlled infrared illumination to observe active or reflective targets while suppressing much of the visible scene. Bright image regions can be detected as blobs and associated with known target points.

Two or more calibrated cameras provide rays whose intersection estimates a point in three dimensions. A rigid arrangement of several points then establishes an object's pose relative to the global tracking frame.

10068.sourceSearchName: information process interpretation of nature information process interpretation of nature
10068.title: Information-Process Interpretation of Nature
10068.heading: Information-Process Interpretation of Nature
10068.content:
An information-process interpretation describes a natural phenomenon through representations, states, transformations, and exchanges. It can make processes in biology, physics, chemistry, and cognition available for computational modeling.

The interpretation is productive when it reproduces observed behavior or generates testable predictions. It should not be confused with proof that the natural system is literally a digital computer.

10070.heading: Document

10071.sourceSearchName: information theoretic metric learning information theoretic metric learning
10071.title: Information-Theoretic Metric Learning
10071.heading: Information-Theoretic Metric Learning
10071.content:
Information-theoretic metric learning finds a Mahalanobis matrix close to an initial metric while satisfying upper bounds for must-link distances and lower bounds for cannot-link distances. LogDet divergence measures the change from the starting geometry.

Efficient Bregman projections enforce pairwise constraints iteratively while preserving positive semidefiniteness. The prior metric therefore supplies a meaningful default that supervision modifies only as much as necessary.

10074.title: Information Utility
10074.heading: Information Utility
10074.content:
Information utility is the property that information is in a usable and useful form for its intended user and purpose. Data may be confidential, correct, authentic, controlled, and available yet still fail if its format, key, context, or representation makes it unusable.

Utility is one of the six properties in the [[Parkerian Hexad]]. Protecting it requires attention to formats, applications, decryption capability, retention, and the consumer's actual information need.

10077.title: Information Theory and Binary Codes
10077.heading: Information Theory and Binary Codes
10077.content:
Information theory gave a mathematical basis for encoding, transmitting, and recovering messages. Binary digits became a common measure because two distinguishable states can express alternatives and combine into larger symbol sets.

The theory developed alongside early digital computers rather than as a consequence of them. Together they made reliable communication and machine representation parts of the same digital system.

10080.sourceSearchName: information storage and distribution information storage and distribution
10080.title: Information Storage and Distribution
10080.heading: Information Storage and Distribution
10080.content:
Information storage and distribution covers retaining data and making it available across systems, organizations, or jurisdictions. Storage affects duration, security, and later reuse, while distribution changes who can interpret or act on the information.

Treating this as a separate activity exposes risks that are hidden when collection and analysis receive all the attention. Copies, remote services, and cross-border transfers can place one dataset under several technical and legal regimes.

10081.sourceSearchName: information storage and distribution information storage and distribution
10081.title: Information Storage and Distribution
10081.heading: References

10083.title: Information Processing
10083.heading: Information Processing
10083.content:
Human information processing is the cycle through which a person senses and interprets stimuli, uses memory and [[Cognition]] to choose a response, performs an action, and perceives resulting [[Feedback]].

Information changes form during this cycle, and each transformation takes time and can introduce errors. [[Attention]] controls which information receives further processing. [[Working Memory]] temporarily holds attended information, while [[Long-Term Memory]] supplies learned concepts, procedures, and past experience.

In interface design, processing time and errors are major contributors to user performance.

10085.sourceSearchName: information possession and control information possession and control
10085.title: Information Possession and Control
10085.heading: Document
10085.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Tags: [[Cloud Security and Data Protection]]

10086.sourceSearchName: information possession and control information possession and control
10086.title: Information Possession and Control
10086.heading: Information Possession and Control
10086.content:
Information possession and control identifies who or what system physically or logically holds information and can determine its immediate use. A party can obtain control of encrypted information without learning its contents, yet can still withhold, destroy, or prevent access to it.

This property is separate from [[Information Confidentiality]]. Cloud storage, backup providers, custodians, and network intermediaries can possess data, so contracts and technical controls should account for their ability to retain or interrupt it.

10087.sourceSearchName: information possession and control information possession and control
10087.title: Information Possession and Control
10087.heading: References

10089.title: Information Gain
10089.heading: Information Gain
10089.content:
Information gain is the entropy of a parent node minus the weighted entropy of the child nodes produced by an attribute split. It is the expected reduction in uncertainty gained by knowing that attribute's value.

ID3 chooses the feature with the largest gain. This often reduces later branching but does not guarantee the globally smallest tree.

10091.sourceSearchName: information layer of play information layer of play
10091.title: Information Layer of Play
10091.heading: Document

10092.sourceSearchName: information layer of play information layer of play
10092.title: Information Layer of Play
10092.heading: Information Layer of Play
10092.content:
The information layer is the player's interpretation of sensory signals as facts about the game state. A perfect information space exposes everything relevant, while an imperfect one deliberately hides some facts through secrecy, fog, uncertainty, or another participant's private knowledge.

More information is not automatically better. The design should reveal enough for intentional decisions while withholding only what supports inference, surprise, bluffing, discovery, or another chosen quality of play.

10095.filePath: 6 - Full Notes/Information Entropy in Decision Trees.md
10095.title: Information Entropy in Decision Trees
10095.heading: Information Entropy in Decision Trees
10095.content:
Information entropy measures the class uncertainty present in a decision-tree node. It is zero when all examples share one class and grows as the class distribution becomes more mixed.

A candidate split is evaluated by the weighted entropy of its child nodes. A useful attribute produces children that are less ambiguous than their parent.

10098.title: Information Filtering
10098.heading: Information Filtering
10098.content:
Information filtering selects which available augmentations should be shown for the current task and context. A knowledge-based filter uses semantic relevance, while a spatial filter uses location, distance, direction, visibility, or the region exposed through an interface such as a magic lens.

Combining both prevents the display from presenting every nearby item merely because it can. The filter reduces data overload while retaining information that matters to the user's purpose.

10100.title: Information Credibility

10101.title: Information Credibility
10101.heading: Information Credibility
10101.content:
Information credibility is the degree to which a claim or source should be considered trustworthy. In social media it can be estimated from message content, source behavior, propagation patterns, and the responses of other users.

Credibility is not equivalent to popularity: repeated sharing can amplify unreliable material. Useful systems expose uncertainty and combine independent evidence rather than treating one network metric as proof.

10103.title: Information Confidentiality
10103.heading: Document
10103.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Security and Data Protection]]

10104.title: Information Confidentiality
10104.heading: Information Confidentiality
10104.content:
Information confidentiality ensures that information is disclosed only to people, applications, or systems authorized to receive it. The required protection depends on the data: intellectual property, financial records, health information, and credentials have different audiences and consequences.

Access control and encryption can support confidentiality, but they apply at different boundaries. Access control decides who may obtain the data, while encryption reduces what an interceptor or unauthorized holder can understand.

10106.sourceSearchName: information borrowing across features information borrowing across features
10106.title: Information Borrowing Across Features

10107.sourceSearchName: information borrowing across features information borrowing across features
10107.title: Information Borrowing Across Features
10107.heading: Information Borrowing Across Features
10107.content:
Information borrowing across features uses the collection of related measurements to stabilize inference for each individual feature. A [[Hierarchical Statistical Model]] estimates the population pattern of feature parameters and uses it to regularize noisy feature-specific estimates.

The approach gains power from high-throughput structure while retaining feature-level results. It assumes the features share a meaningful parameter distribution, not that their observed values or biological effects are identical.

10109.title: Information Availability
10109.heading: Document
10109.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Security and Data Protection]]

10110.title: Information Availability
10110.heading: Information Availability
10110.content:
Information availability means that authorized users can obtain information or a service in time for its intended purpose. It includes reach from required locations, readiness when requested, continuity during demand, and recovery after failure.

Availability commitments can distinguish planned downtime, service restoration time, and tolerable data loss. [[Recovery Time Objective]] and [[Recovery Point Objective]] give measurable targets for the last two concerns.

10112.title: Information Authenticity
10112.heading: Document
10112.content:
2026-09-08 22:39

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Cloud Security and Data Protection]]

10113.title: Information Authenticity
10113.heading: Information Authenticity
10113.content:
Information authenticity is confidence that information genuinely originated or was created where it claims. It concerns the veracity of the source, not only whether the contents remained unchanged afterward.

Establishing identity, validating credentials or certificates, and protecting messages against substitution support authenticity. It complements [[Data Integrity]] because an unmodified message can still be inauthentic if it came from an impostor.

10116.sourceSearchName: information as a service information as a service
10116.title: Information as a Service
10116.heading: Information as a Service
10116.content:
Information as a service delivers data that has been transformed or selected so that it is meaningful to a consumer's situation. Raw storage is not sufficient; software must add context such as current location, applicable rules, relevant prices, or a timely interpretation.

An information service builds on lower cloud layers and exposes defined interfaces to other applications. Its quality depends on currency, accuracy, relevance, privacy, and the consumer's ability to understand how the supplied information should be used.

10117.title: Information as a Service

10119.title: Influence Decay
10119.heading: Influence Decay
10119.content:
Influence decay models the reduction in a topic's effect as time passes after reports or interactions. A decay function can weight recent activity more strongly while retaining accumulated influence from earlier periods.

The rate need not be constant; it can change with attention and reporting frequency. Including decay helps a popularity model avoid treating old and current evidence as equally predictive.

10122.content:
Infectious disease prediction uses health records and surveillance observations to estimate where or when disease activity may increase. Combining sources can reveal temporal and geographic patterns earlier than isolated reports.

Predictions depend on timely reporting, consistent definitions, and awareness of bias in who is observed. A model supports monitoring and response but does not replace epidemiological interpretation.

10125.title: Inference Complexity
10125.heading: Inference Complexity
10125.content:
Inference complexity is the computational cost of answering a question from a probabilistic description. It is shaped by the searched and free variables, their domains, and the dependencies created during marginalization.

A compact model is not automatically easy to query. Good decompositions expose conditional independences that keep intermediate calculations small, while an unfortunate query or elimination order can still cause rapid growth.

10128.title: Infection Snapshot
10128.heading: Infection Snapshot
10128.content:
An infection snapshot records which network nodes occupy diffusion states at one observation time. It provides a cross-section of the spread but usually omits exact transmission paths and activation times.

Source estimators infer backward from this incomplete result. Different origins can create similar snapshots, especially under recovery, missing observations, variable edge rates, or multiple sources.

10131.heading: Inertial Confinement Fusion
10131.content: Inertial confinement fusion compresses a small deuterium-tritium fuel pellet with a brief, intense laser pulse. The fuel reaches extreme density and temperature and reacts during the short interval before it expands. No sustained magnetic chamber is needed for that event, unlike [[Magnetic Fusion Confinement]]. A power plant would still have to repeat the process and collect useful heat from the reactions.

10134.title: Inertial Navigation Drift
10134.heading: Inertial Navigation Drift
10134.content: Inertial navigation derives velocity and position by integrating measurements from gyroscopes and accelerometers. Small sensor biases and alignment errors are integrated along with real motion, so the estimated state gradually diverges from the true state. The system is self-contained, passive, and immune to radio jamming, but it periodically needs an external position fix unless its mission is short. Satellite measurements and inertial estimates therefore complement one another: one supplies absolute correction and the other continuity.

Error grows with time as sensor bias is integrated, making inertial equipment a continuity layer rather than a permanent replacement for external fixes.

Pose must be inferred by integrating its relative measurements, which accumulates drift. AR systems therefore commonly combine inertial responsiveness with slower absolute evidence from cameras or other sensors.

10143.title: Inequality
10143.heading: Inequality
10143.content:
An inequality compares two expressions by order rather than asserting that they are equal. The relations less than, greater than, less than or equal to, and greater than or equal to are written (<), (>), (\leq), and (\geq).

An inequality with a variable usually describes a [[Solution Set of an Inequality]] containing many values. Equality-preserving methods still help isolate the variable, but multiplication or division by a negative value reverses the relation. The result can be represented as an [[Interval]] and graphed on a [[Number Line]].

10146.title: Inequality Symbol
10146.heading: Inequality Symbol
10146.content:
An inequality symbol states the ordering relationship between two quantities:

- (a<b): (a) is less than (b)
- (a>b): (a) is greater than (b)
- (a\leq b): (a) is less than or equal to (b)
- (a\geq b): (a) is greater than or equal to (b)

The strict symbols exclude equality, while the inclusive symbols permit it. On a graph, that difference is shown through an [[Open Endpoint]] or [[Closed Endpoint]]. Reversing the order of the two expressions also reverses the symbol: (a<b) is equivalent to (b>a).

10149.title: Industry 4.0
10149.heading: Industry 4.0
10149.content:
Industry 4.0 describes an industrial stage built around connected machines, cyber-physical systems, pervasive data, and increasingly autonomous production. Sensors and networked equipment allow processes to be monitored and adjusted through analytics.

The concept links physical operations to [[Business Intelligence and Analytics 4.0]]. Automation therefore depends on both machine connectivity and methods capable of converting streams of operational data into decisions.

10152.title: Inductive Reactance
10152.heading: Inductive Reactance
10152.content: Inductive reactance is the opposition an ideal inductor presents to sinusoidal current, $X_L=\omega L$. It increases with frequency because rapidly changing current induces a larger back emf. In an ideal inductor, current lags voltage by one quarter cycle, and energy is stored and returned rather than dissipated on average.

10155.title: Inductive Bias in Machine Learning
10155.heading: Inductive Bias in Machine Learning
10155.content:
Inductive bias is the set of assumptions a learning algorithm uses to prefer some functions over others beyond what the examples alone establish. A model restricted to straight-line relationships, for instance, assumes linear structure even when the dataset might also support more complex mappings.

The bias counterbalances the [[Ill-Posed Learning Problem|ambiguity of learning from limited examples]]. If it is too restrictive for the domain, the chosen function may [[Model Underfitting|underfit]]; if it is too permissive relative to the available data, it may [[Model Overfitting|overfit]] noise. Kelleher describes neural networks as having relatively weak bias, which helps them learn flexible relationships but also increases their demand for substantial data.

An induced pluripotent stem cell is a mature donor cell reprogrammed into a state capable of generating many specialized cell types. It allows researchers to derive tissue-relevant cells while retaining the donor's genetic background.

10161.title: Induced Fuzziness
10161.heading: Induced Fuzziness
10161.content:
Induced fuzziness transforms numeric or crisp attribute values into graded linguistic memberships before further analysis. A continuous height, for example, can have partial membership in several labels instead of one abrupt category.

The transformation uses a family of membership functions and should preserve distinctions relevant to the application. Its thresholds and shapes become part of the data representation.

10164.title: Induced and Parasite Drag
10164.heading: Induced and Parasite Drag
10164.content: Induced drag is the drag associated with producing lift and is especially important at lower speeds and higher lift coefficients. Parasite drag combines form, skin-friction, and interference effects and grows strongly as speed increases. Their opposing speed trends create a minimum in total drag that helps define efficient cruise and glide conditions.

10167.title: Individual View
10167.heading: Individual View
10167.content:
An individual view presents shared augmented content from one participant's physical viewpoint and may also contain information private to that participant. Head or device tracking generates the correct perspective even when several users surround the same objects.

Individual views support role-specific detail and avoid forcing everyone to see one projected image. Collaboration cues must still reveal relevant actions and attention so private presentation does not remove awareness of the group.

10170.title: Individual Preference
10170.heading: Individual Preference
10170.content:
Individual preference describes how well an item's topics or semantics match a user's interests. It can be estimated by comparing the item's topic distribution with the distributions of items the user previously adopted.

Preference is one contextual factor in [[Social Recommendation]]. A user may still adopt a weakly preferred item because influential friends sent it, or reject a preferred item when it lacks visibility or trusted endorsement.

10173.title: Individual Autonomy
10173.heading: Individual Autonomy
10173.content:
Individual autonomy is the capacity to form purposes and direct one's own life. Privacy supports this capacity by limiting continuous observation and preserving room for reflection, experimentation, and choice.

In a Big Data environment, autonomy can be affected even without direct coercion. Persistent profiling and prediction may shape options or behavior, so the legal question includes how information systems alter the conditions under which choices are made.

10176.sourceSearchName: indirect duties to machines indirect duties to machines
10176.title: Indirect Duties to Machines
10176.heading: Indirect Duties to Machines
10176.content:
Indirect duties to machines are obligations concerning how people treat artificial systems even when the systems themselves have no rights or experiences. Abusing a humanlike robot may cultivate cruelty, distress observers, or normalize harmful patterns of behavior toward beings that resemble social partners.

On this account, the immediate beneficiary of the duty is human character or social life rather than the machine. It offers a reason to regulate treatment without first proving [[Machine Sentience]]. The approach differs from [[Relational Moral Status]], which treats the relationship with the machine itself as capable of grounding moral consideration.

10179.title: Indicator Variable
10179.heading: Indicator Variable
10179.content:
An indicator variable encodes membership in a category with 1 for the focal state and 0 for the comparison state. It lets a regression coefficient describe the contrast between that state and the [[Regression Reference Group]].

A categorical variable with several levels is commonly represented by several indicators while one level is omitted as the reference. Analysts should verify every indicator against its source category and avoid treating unreported values as a meaningful comparison group without justification.

In the source's design matrices, an indicator column marks whether each experimental unit belongs to a treatment or factor level. The associated coefficient becomes a difference from the omitted reference condition, making coding choices part of the model's scientific interpretation.

10185.heading: Indicated, Calibrated, Equivalent, and True Airspeed

Calibrated airspeed corrects instrument and position error, equivalent airspeed further corrects compressibility effects, and true airspeed corrects for the actual atmospheric density. 10188.heading: Indexed Mesh Representation
10188.content:
An indexed mesh stores each reusable vertex once and defines faces by referring to positions in that vertex list. Normals and texture coordinates may have their own indexed collections, allowing the representation to share data where appropriate.

Compared with a naive specification that repeats every triangle's coordinates, indexing can substantially reduce file size and reveal which faces share geometric points. It also introduces ordering dependencies: a face remains meaningful only while its indices correspond to the intended entries in the referenced lists.

10197.title: Independent Malware
10197.heading: Independent Malware
10197.content:
Independent malware is a self-contained malicious program rather than code attached to a host file. A [[Computer Worm]] can execute and propagate on its own, and remotely controlled systems can become a [[Zombie Computer]] within a [[Botnet]].

This independence enables rapid network-scale activity. Defenses therefore combine patching and endpoint controls with segmentation, network monitoring, traffic restriction, and fast containment of compromised devices.

10200.title: Incremental Funding
10200.heading: Incremental Funding
10200.content:
Incremental funding releases capital for a project in stages tied to subprojects, evidence, or delivered capabilities. An organization can learn from early work before committing the full portfolio cost.

The sequence changes when expenses occur and when benefits begin, so it can change net present value even when the same components are eventually completed.

10203.title: Incremental Backup
10203.heading: Incremental Backup
10203.content:
An incremental backup copies new or changed files since the previous incremental backup. The first set establishes a complete baseline, and each subsequent set records only the next changes.

Incrementals reduce backup time and storage and can preserve several versions across sets. Complete restoration requires the baseline and every necessary increment in order, so a missing or damaged set can interrupt the recovery chain.

Incremental function development begins with working expressions and moves them into a function in small, testable steps. Each parameter or branch is introduced only after the previous behavior is understood.

This approach keeps debugging local and makes it easier to compare the function's result with the original interactive analysis.

Row reduction exposes inconsistency when an [[Augmented Matrix]] contains a row with all zero coefficients but a nonzero right-hand side. No choice of the unknown vector can satisfy such an equation.

10212.title: Incompressible Flow
10212.heading: Incompressible Flow
10212.content:
Incompressible flow assumes a fluid parcel has no volume change, so density remains constant and the velocity field has zero divergence. Liquids are often approximated this way in potential-flow analysis.

The constraint links spatial velocity components and permits scalar potential or stream-function formulations under additional assumptions. It does not by itself imply zero viscosity or zero rotation.

10215.title: Incomplete Data
10215.heading: Incomplete Data
10215.content:
Incomplete data omits values for variables that participate in a probabilistic model. Treating the missing values as latent variables allows their possibilities to be inferred rather than silently discarded or filled with unjustified constants.

Parameter learning then depends on both observed evidence and uncertainty about what was not observed. Expectation-maximization is one method for alternating between those two parts of the problem.

10218.title: Inclusive AI Development
10218.heading: Inclusive AI Development
10218.content:
Inclusive AI development brings varied social positions, disciplines, and affected communities into the design and evaluation of an AI system. Homogeneous teams are more likely to overlook assumptions, missing populations, and harms outside their own experience.

Inclusion is more than adding demographic diversity to a technical team. People who bear the consequences need meaningful influence over problem definition, acceptable risk, and deployment. Their knowledge can reveal failures that aggregate performance measures hide. The practice connects [[Bias Mitigation in AI]] with [[Stakeholder Participation in AI Governance]].

10221.content:
Inclusive game design broadens participation by removing unnecessary barriers while preserving a coherent identity and purpose. It differs from trying to make one game universal through an unrelated mixture of features.

Designers should research the chosen audience, question binary demographic assumptions, and avoid exclusionary material that does not serve the core experience. Inclusion is a disciplined fit between people and design, not a promise that everyone will like the same game.

10224.title: Incident Retrospective
10224.heading: Incident Retrospective
10224.content:
An incident retrospective reconstructs the timeline, contributing conditions, available signals, responses, and recovery after a live failure. Its purpose is to strengthen the system, not identify a person to blame.

Useful outcomes include clearer detection, safer deployment, new tests, reduced response time, and changes to organizational conditions. The review turns operational failure into shared product knowledge.

The arrangement is the default Windows hosting model described for current ASP.NET Core versions in the source. It contrasts with [[Out-of-Process Hosting]], which separates the reverse proxy and application server processes.

10230.heading: In-Memory Database
10230.content:
An in-memory database treats main memory as the primary location for database operations. Its indexes, layouts, and query paths can avoid assumptions inherited from slower block storage.

Durability still requires a strategy such as logging, replication, or periodic snapshots. The performance gain therefore comes from keeping the common execution path in memory, not from pretending failures cannot occur.

EF Core's testing provider supplies a disposable in-process database whose changing state can be isolated for each automated test. The book distinguishes this convenient application test from a narrow unit test and notes that real database operations are otherwise slow and difficult to repeat.

10233.title: In-Memory Database Provider
10233.heading: In-Memory Database Provider
10233.content:
An in-memory database provider stores test data in process instead of connecting Entity Framework Core to the production database server. It gives a test a fast, disposable context with known records.

This supports isolated controller tests without a SQL Server dependency. Because the provider does not reproduce every relational database behavior, it is a unit-testing aid rather than proof that production SQL integration works identically.

The web-research tests configure a uniquely named EF Core in-memory database through `DbContextOptionsBuilder`. The real context type is then supplied to a controller, allowing create-and-retrieve behavior to be exercised without a persistent SQL Server instance.

10236.title: In-Memory Data Grid
10236.heading: In-Memory Data Grid
10236.content:
An in-memory data grid distributes key-value or object data across the memory of multiple machines. Partitioning and replication provide a shared data space that can grow beyond one server while keeping access faster than disk-oriented storage.

Applications can place computation near partitions, but concurrent updates require consistency, isolation, and failure-recovery mechanisms across nodes.

10239.title: In-Memory Computing
10239.heading: In-Memory Computing
10239.content:
In-memory computing keeps active data and intermediate state in main memory so processors avoid repeated disk access. It is especially useful for interactive, iterative, and streaming workloads whose latency is dominated by storage transfers.

Memory residence does not remove the need for durability, distribution, or recovery. Systems must decide what to replicate, checkpoint, or reconstruct after a failure.
